title: Acute Cardiovascular, Handgrip Strength, and Perceptual Responses to a Grappling-Based Operational Restraint Simulation in Tactical Law Enforcement Trainees: A Pilot Study
content: Background/Objectives: Physical control of a resistant person imposes substantial cardiovascular and upper-limb demands, yet integrated evidence from grappling-based law-enforcement restraint tasks is limited. This pilot study characterized acute responses and explored associations with physical fitness. Methods: Thirty male tactical law enforcement trainees formed 15 two-person patrols. Physical fitness was assessed 48 h before the simulation using push-up, pull-up, sit-up, and 12 min Cooper tests. Heart rate and handgrip strength were assessed before and during the immediate post-simulation sequence, with Borg CR10 recorded at its end. Paired t-tests evaluated acute changes; 12 exploratory Spearman correlations were FDR-adjusted, with patrol-aggregated sensitivity analyses. Results: Heart rate increased from 74.2 ± 11.5 to 142.9 ± 27.0 beats·min⁻¹ (p < 0.001; d = 2.73). Dominant- and non-dominant-hand handgrip strength decreased by 5.67 kg (p < 0.001; d = −1.14) and 3.66 kg (p = 0.002; d = −0.63). Borg CR10 was 7.1 ± 2.0 and median completion time was 435 s. Higher pull-up performance was associated with lower perceived exertion and better handgrip preservation, while higher push-up performance was associated with lower perceived exertion; sensitivity analyses supported these patterns except for non-dominant-hand handgrip preservation. Conclusions: The simulation was accompanied by marked cardiovascular activation, bilateral reductions in handgrip strength, and high perceived exertion. These pilot findings characterize key acute demands of two-officer operational restraint and support further investigation of upper-body muscular endurance in task tolerance.
